Neighbor's Tree Damaged Your Fence? California Law Explained
Three words cost California homeowners thousands every storm season: "act of God."
When a neighbor's tree falls on your fence, California applies a negligence standard. The tree owner usually pays only if they knew, or should have known, the tree was dangerous: visible rot, dead branches, a serious lean, or earlier limb failures.
Under Civil Code Section 833, a tree belongs to the owner of the land where its trunk stands. Section 834 makes boundary trees shared property. And Section 841, California's Good Neighbor Fence Law, presumes neighbors share responsibility for boundary fences.
That's why documentation matters: dated photos, written notes to the neighbor, and an arborist's assessment of concerning trees. Coverage matters too. A fence damaged by a falling tree may fall under the other structures part of a homeowners policy, subject to the deductible.

Mobile home residents in California own the home while renting the land beneath it, and that split creates costs many buyers never see coming: annual lot rent increases, HOA fees, utility pass through charges for park upgrades, setup and hookup fees, and resale restrictions written into park leases.
